questions.q: What do Lesson 10's and Lesson 11's mistakes actually have in common?
options: They both happened in the same AWS region
Both changes went through a pull request whose checks validated syntax and plan success, but nothing inspected what the change would actually do
They were both caused by the same person
Neither mistake went through any review process at all
questions.explain: Both mistakes passed existing checks because those checks never looked at the actual content of the change -- just whether it would apply cleanly.

questions.q: What does the new 'Terraform Plan (JSON)' step produce that the guardrail script needs?
options: A human-readable plan summary only
A structured JSON version of the plan (via terraform show -json) that a script can inspect programmatically
A screenshot of the Terraform CLI output
A list of all files changed in the pull request
questions.explain: terraform show -json converts the plan into structured data the guardrail script can actually parse and check against rules.

questions.q: What does the replica-count guardrail check for, and what lets it pass anyway?
options: It blocks any minReplicas value above 4, with no way to override it
It flags a minReplicas value above 4 unless the pull request carries a deliberate 'peak-season-override' label
It only checks maxReplicas, never minReplicas
It automatically fixes the value without asking anyone
questions.explain: The check isn't a hard ban -- it requires a visible, intentional override label for a legitimate high-floor case, rather than letting it ship silently.

questions.q: What does the bucket-policy guardrail check for?
options: Whether the bucket has versioning enabled
A policy statement granting Principal "*" with no Condition attached
Whether the bucket name follows a naming convention
Whether the bucket is in the correct AWS region
questions.explain: This check would have failed Lesson 6's original pull request before the bucket was ever created with a wildcard-principal policy.

questions.q: How does a failed guardrail actually stop a bad change from shipping?
options: It only posts an informational comment; the merge button still works
It exits non-zero, failing the CI job, which — combined with branch protection requiring that status check — blocks the merge button entirely
It emails an administrator who manually reverts the change later
It automatically deletes the pull request
questions.explain: A loud, blocking failure tied to branch protection is what actually prevents the merge, unlike a warning-only comment that still lets it through.
